newsitem.title: UK: Russian workers starved on "Adolf Island".
newsitem.headline: Russian workers starved on "Adolf Island".

text.p: Russians forced to work for the Germans occupying the Channel Islands during World War Two were perpetually beaten and so hungry that they were forced to dig up the rotting entrails of dead animals for food.
One naked prisoner was crucified on the camp gates in winter and guards threw water over him all night until he died.

Official reports released in Britain on Tuesday reveal the brutal treatment meted out to the foreign labourers, mainly Russians, who were forced to build fortifications around the Channel Islands, the only part of Britain Germany succeeded in occupying in either of the two world wars.
The Germans ran a concentration camp on one of the smaller islands, Alderney, which they renamed Adolf Island. Around 900 political prisoners and 600 Jews were imprisoned there.
The prisoners were starved, beaten and even killed without compunction, according to the papers released by the Public Record Office.
Informants described how prison guards used bloodhounds to chase prisoners across the camp's boundary lines so that they would be shot by the sentries.
"This was the favourite method of the SS to get rid of prisoners they disliked," said one.

Although weak with hunger and malnutrition, the prisoners were forced to work digging trenches and building fortifications around the islands which Adolf Hitler refused to accept had no strategic value.
But their fate was no worse than that of the thousands of foreign workers.
They worked 12 hours a day on a diet of watery cabbage soup and a little bread. If they flagged they were beaten with whips, spade handles or rubber hoses filled with sand.
At least half of the 1,600 workers sent to Alderney either starved or were beaten to death.
Under German regulations they should have been fed the same rations as the soldiers, but those in charge on Alderney diverted their food into the military's kitchens.

"It is clear why the leading personalities looked so well and were able to indulge in orgies with specially imported foreign prostitutes," one German prisoner-of-war told a British military interviewer in one report.
"I have seen undernourished Russians forced by hunger digging up buried intestines of slaughtered animals with their bare hands behind the slaughter house to satisfy their hunger," said another.
In June 1943, a German commission was sent to Alderney to find out why the occupying force was claiming rations for 600 more workers than they had.
The investigators were shocked to find only 800 workers still alive. They sent 450 of them to hospital and returned the remainder to do light duties in France.
Two German officers were arrested, although the reports do not make clear what happened to them.
Some of the workers were volunteers but most of them were sent by Nazi-occupied villages and towns forced to provide quotas of labourers.

The British defence ministry reports have been kept secret for more than 50 years because Germany had been trying to decide whether they contained enough information to prosecute a senior SS officer who served on Alderney.
